fields.problem:
Title: all poly's such that $P(n)$ divides $2^n-1$

Find all polynomials $P$ with integer coefficients such that $P(n)$ divides $2^n-1$ for all positive integers $n$.

Context (from a comment by the OP): it's my own problem formulated while I was reading articles on Mersenne primes, I don't have any results (neither mine nor founded)
fields.source_context:
0001 | Here’s another proof, which I believe is simpler. Let $P \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ be such a polynomial. Then, note that $P(n)|P(2n)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
0002 | 
0003 | Lemma
0004 | 
0005 | Let $f, g \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ be s.t. $g(n)|f(n)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then, $f = rg$ for some $r \in \mathbb{Z}$.
0006 | 
0007 | Proof (sketch)
0008 | 
0009 | Write:
0010 | 
0011 | $$f(x) = a_kx^k + \cdots + a_0$$
0012 | $$g(x) = b_lx^l + \cdots + b_0$$
0013 | 
0014 | By considering the limiting behaviour of the ratio as $n \to \infty$, clearly we must have that $k = l$. We also deduce that $\frac{a_k}{b_k} = r \in \mathbb{Z}$.
0015 | 
0016 | Let $D$ denote the difference operator which acts as $(Df)(n) = f(n+1) - f(n)$. Note that if $f(n) = rg(n)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $(D^j f)(n) = r(D^jg)(n)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. We conclude the proof by induction on $j$ with the claim that $D^j f = r D^j g \implies D^{(j-1)} f = r D^{(j-1)}g$.
0017 |
fields.witness: f = X² − 1 and g = X + 1 in ℤ[x]. For every natural n, g(n) = n + 1 divides f(n) = (n + 1)(n − 1), with cofactor n − 1. If f = r·g for a constant r ∈ ℤ, evaluating at n = 0 gives −1 = r and at n = 1 gives 0 = 2r, which is impossible. So no constant r works (the actual quotient is the non-constant polynomial X − 1).
